content.title: How to Watch the Northern Lights from 10 States Tonight
content.text: The Northern Lights are seen in Cudjoe Key near Key West. Credit : Jen Golbeck/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty NEED TO KNOW A coronal mass ejection may spark faint northern lights late March 26 into early March 27Viewing is best in northern states like Alaska, Montana and Michigan with clear skies and low light pollutionThe equinox effect enhances auroras by allowing solar particles to interact more easily with Earth's magnetic field Keep your eyes on the sky tonight, because the northern lights are making a comeback! After weeks of heightened geomagnetic activity tied to the spring equinox, Earth’s magnetic field has begun to settle, but this doesn’t mean the aurora show is over just yet. For reference, the northern lights (aurora borealis) are caused by geomagnetic storms, which occur when charged particles from the sun collide with gases in Earth's atmosphere, creating brilliant waves of light in the sky. Still, their visibility depends on several factors, including intensity and location. According to NOAA Space weather forecasters, a coronal mass ejection (CME) could pass near Earth late this evening, March 26, into early Friday, March 27. Recent solar activity included a moderate flare and lingering solar wind streams, adding just enough momentum to keep things interesting. While models suggest the majority of this solar energy could miss us, even a slight interaction with Earth is enough to spark faint auroras. This is especially true when considering the “equinox effect,” when Earth’s magnetic field is positioned in a way that allows charged particles from the sun to more easily interact with our planet’s magnetosphere. Here’s everything you need to know about when, where and how to watch this stellar event. Related Stories When will the northern lights be visible? The aurora borealis. Li Hongjun/VCG via Getty I If auroras develop, the most likely viewing window will be late Thursday, March 26, into the early hours of Friday, March 27. NOAA forecasters say geomagnetic conditions could briefly reach unsettled-to-active levels, with isolated minor G1 storm periods possible before activity gradually quiets down. Where will the northern lights be visible? The northern lights. Getty The strongest chances are expected across northern states closest to the Canadian border. Potential viewing areas include Alaska, Washington, Idaho, Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, Minnesota, Wisconsin, Michigan, and Maine. Still, if geomagnetic activity intensifies, the aurora could extend slightly farther south into parts of New York, New Hampshire, and Vermont, though displays there would be faint and difficult to see without a camera. How to watch the northern lights? Aurora borealis display near Fairbanks. Gallo Images ROOTS Collection/Getty The key is to find a spot away from city lights using a light pollution map or a dark-sky finder. You’ll also need a clear northern sky and patience!Remember, auroras are inherently unpredictable and often come in waves. Keep checking live forecasts throughout the evening, as conditions can shift minute by minute. How to photograph the northern lights? Photographer on Skagsanden capturing the Northern Lights. Getty You don’t need professional gear to capture the auroras... but it certainly helps! If you're hoping to photograph the northern lights, you'll want to keep your setup as steady as possible, since the auroras are best captured with long exposures. But if you have a smartphone handy, that works just fine. All you have to do is head to your device's settings and tap the "Night Mode" option or “Pro Mode,” which offers similar exposure times.
